transistor-name-off-patent-1947.title: The Name Left Off the Patent
transistor-name-off-patent-1947.body: On December 23, 1947, Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated a germanium point-contact transistor at Bell Labs. Shockley was not in the room. Lawyers found his own design too close to a 1925 patent by Julius Lilienfeld and dropped his name from this one.
transistor-name-off-patent-1947.coda: In 1956 all three shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.

dartmouth-two-month-study-1956.title: A Two-Month Study
dartmouth-two-month-study-1956.body: The 1955 proposal by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon asked for a two-month, ten-man study, on the premise that intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. The 1956 workshop ran six to eight weeks; only three attendees stayed the whole time.
dartmouth-two-month-study-1956.coda: The name they picked for the field, artificial intelligence, is the one that stuck.

traitorous-eight-lie-detector-1957.title: The Lie Detector Memo
traitorous-eight-lie-detector-1957.body: In May 1957, eight engineers at Shockley Semiconductor demanded William Shockley be replaced as manager. He had recorded phone calls, blocked staff from sharing results, and required lie-detector tests. On September 18, 1957, the eight founded Fairchild Semiconductor instead.
traitorous-eight-lie-detector-1957.coda: Wikipedia counts Intel and AMD among the dozens of companies traced back to that spinoff.

kilby-noyce-six-months-1958-1959.title: Six Months, One Medal
kilby-noyce-six-months-1958-1959.body: Kilby demonstrated a working integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in September 1958, its parts joined by external wires. Noyce filed a monolithic silicon version at Fairchild in July 1959, mass-producible. Neither man rejected the other's claim to co-inventor.
kilby-noyce-six-months-1958-1959.coda: Kilby accepted the 2000 Nobel Prize alone. Noyce had died in 1990.

perceptron-conscious-machine-1958.title: The Machine That Would Wake Up
perceptron-conscious-machine-1958.body: In 1958 the New York Times reported that Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron was the embryo of a computer the Navy expected to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence. In 1969 Minsky and Papert's book proved a single-layer perceptron could not compute XOR.
perceptron-conscious-machine-1958.coda: Funding for neural network research dried up and did not return until the 1980s.

hamilton-software-engineering.title: An Ongoing Joke
hamilton-software-engineering.body: During the Apollo program, Margaret Hamilton began calling her work "software engineering" to distinguish it from hardware engineering. She said no one had heard the term before and it became an ongoing joke, until a respected hardware engineer stood up in a meeting and agreed.
hamilton-software-engineering.coda: The joke ran for years, then nobody told it anymore.

macau-seventeen-thousand.title: Seventeen thousand
macau-seventeen-thousand.body: In October 1961 a syndicate formed by Stanley Ho, Henry Fok, Yip Hon and Teddy Yip bid for the Macau gaming monopoly. They offered 3,167,000 patacas, seventeen thousand more than the rival bid.
macau-seventeen-thousand.coda: The monopoly that margin bought them held for more than forty years.

moores-law-ten-year-bet-1965.title: A Ten-Year Bet
moores-law-ten-year-bet-1965.body: Moore's 1965 article predicted the component count on a chip would double every year for the next decade, reaching roughly 65,000 by 1975. In 1975 he revised the doubling period to two years. The curve later called a law was his own forecast, already amended once.
moores-law-ten-year-bet-1965.coda: By 1995 Moore said the term had come to mean almost anything in the chip industry.

eliza-secretary-1966.title: The Secretary and DOCTOR
eliza-secretary-1966.body: In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum released ELIZA's DOCTOR script at MIT, a program that mostly reflected users' own sentences back as questions. His own secretary reportedly asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it alone.
eliza-secretary-1966.coda: The pattern he had not expected was later named the ELIZA effect.

engelbart-royalties.title: Forty thousand dollars
engelbart-royalties.body: SRI patented the mouse after the demo and, by its own account, had no real idea of its value. Some years later it emerged that they had licensed it to Apple for something like $40,000.
engelbart-royalties.coda: Engelbart never received any royalties for inventing it.

lo.title: LO
lo.body: Charley Kline set out to log in to a machine at SRI from UCLA. The L arrived. The O arrived. On the G the far end crashed.
lo.coda: The first thing ever said on the internet was two letters: LO.

multics.title: Computing as a utility
multics.body: Multics was not designed as a computer but as a computing utility: always on, the way power is, with the tenants of one machine sealed off from each other. It shipped late and expensive, and Bell Labs walked away.
multics.coda: Fifty years later the idea was renamed cloud computing.

rfc1.title: Request for Comments
rfc1.body: Steve Crocker had to write the first rules for a few networked hosts. Nobody had given him the authority, and he feared it would read as pulling rank — so he called the genre a Request for Comments.
rfc1.coda: Every rule the internet has agreed on since is still called an RFC.

pdp7.title: The machine nobody wanted
pdp7.body: After Bell Labs quit Multics, Ken Thompson had a cast-off PDP-7 and a month alone while his wife and son were in San Diego. He gave himself a week per piece: kernel, shell, editor, assembler.
pdp7.coda: Four weeks later the machine nobody wanted was running Unix.

alarm-1202.title: Program alarm 1202
alarm-1202.body: Four minutes from the surface the guidance computer raised five alarms: a rendezvous radar switch left in the wrong position was eating its cycles. It did not hang. It shed the low-priority jobs, restarted, and kept the landing.
alarm-1202.coda: Knowing what to drop under load is the expensive lesson.

mariner-1.title: One missing overbar
mariner-1.body: Mariner 1 was destroyed 293 seconds after launch. An onboard beacon had failed, and when the guidance equations were copied into the program an overbar was dropped from R. The bar meant take the average.
mariner-1.coda: The press found overbar hard to explain and wrote hyphen. The hyphen stuck.

mother-of-all-demos.title: The Mother of All Demos
mother-of-all-demos.body: Engelbart was given ninety minutes. His terminal ran over telephone lines to a machine thirty miles away, and he demonstrated the mouse, hyperlinks, windows, screen sharing, and two people editing one document at once.
mother-of-all-demos.coda: A thousand people watched, then went back to punch cards for another decade.

conway.title: The paper that was turned down
conway.body: Melvin Conway wrote up the observation that a system's structure ends up mirroring the communication structure of the organisation that built it, and sent "How Do Committees Invent?" to Harvard Business Review. They rejected it on the grounds that he had not proved his thesis. Datamation ran it in 1968.
conway.coda: Fred Brooks later cited the unproven thesis and named it Conway's law.

apollo-burn-baby-burn.title: Burn, Baby, Burn
apollo-burn-baby-burn.body: The lunar module's master ignition routine is labelled BURN_BABY_BURN in the source. The name is not about the thrust; it was borrowed from a soul radio DJ's catchphrase of the day.
apollo-burn-baby-burn.coda: The line still sits unedited in the public repository.

waterfall.title: The diagram was the counterexample
waterfall.body: In "Managing the Development of Large Software Systems" Winston Royce drew the chart the industry would come to call the waterfall model, then wrote: "I believe in this concept, but the implementation described above is risky and invites failure." The rest of the paper is about making it iterative.
waterfall.coda: The industry kept the diagram and dropped the sentence.

moth.title: The first actual bug
moth.body: A moth was pulled from a relay of the Harvard Mark II and taped into the logbook. The line beside it is cited as the origin of the word, but what it says is: first actual case of bug being found.
moth.coda: Engineers had said bug since Edison. The museum doubts the page is even in Hopper's hand.

intel-4004-busicom-rights-1971.title: A Chip Owned by a Calculator Company
intel-4004-busicom-rights-1971.body: In 1969 Japan's Busicom commissioned Intel to design a calculator chipset, under a contract assigning the design rights to Busicom despite the work being done entirely inside Intel. In 1971 engineer Federico Faggin traded a lower price for release from that exclusivity.
intel-4004-busicom-rights-1971.coda: General sales of the Intel 4004 began that July.

pong-coin-overflow.title: The Coin Box Overflowed
pong-coin-overflow.body: In August 1972, Atari placed the Pong prototype in a bar in Sunnyvale. A few days later the owner reported it broken. Engineer Al Alcorn drove out to fix it and found the fault was not electrical: the coin mechanism had jammed because it was overflowing with quarters.
pong-coin-overflow.coda: The malfunction was not a wiring fault; it was too many coins.

wozniak-breakout-bonus.title: The Split
wozniak-breakout-bonus.body: In 1973 Atari asked Steve Jobs to shrink the Breakout circuit board, paying $100 per chip removed. Jobs asked Wozniak to help, promising half. Wozniak cut 50 chips. Jobs said the total came to $700, so Wozniak's share was $350. Ten years later Wozniak learned the real bonus was $5,000.
wozniak-breakout-bonus.coda: Wozniak said he would have given Jobs the money if asked.

unix-not-expected-to-understand.title: Not Expected to Understand
unix-not-expected-to-understand.body: Sixth Edition Unix's slp.c contains the line 'You are not expected to understand this,' attached to process-swap stack-restoration code built on PDP-11 compiler quirks. Dennis Ritchie later said he meant it the way a teacher says this won't be on the exam.
unix-not-expected-to-understand.coda: The routine was rewritten for Seventh Edition Unix.

vi-adm3a-keys.title: Arrows Inscribed on Letter Keys
vi-adm3a-keys.body: Bill Joy wrote vi at Berkeley in 1977 on a Lear Siegler ADM-3A terminal that had no arrow keys; h, j, k and l were inscribed with arrows and became the movement keys. The terse one-letter commands came from typing ahead of a 300-baud modem too slow to keep up.
vi-adm3a-keys.coda: The keys later credited to design philosophy began as a workaround for a terminal with no arrow keys.

kildall-flying.title: The Flight That Wasn't Confirmed
kildall-flying.body: In 1980 IBM came to license CP/M. Gary Kildall was flying software to a client; his wife Dorothy handled the opening talks. Bill Gates later told reporters Kildall had "capriciously gone flying." IBM's lead negotiator, Jack Sams, said he never met Kildall at all.
kildall-flying.coda: The two accounts of that meeting have never been reconciled.

trusting-trust.title: Reflections on Trusting Trust
trusting-trust.body: Thompson's Turing lecture described a compiler that plants a backdoor in the login program, and reinstalls the entire trick whenever it compiles a compiler. Rebuild from clean source and the backdoor survives.
trusting-trust.coda: You cannot trust code you did not totally create yourself.

arm-one-person-company-1985.title: A One-Person Chip Company
arm-one-person-company-1985.body: Acorn, which had made its name on education computers, began RISC research in 1983. A visit to a rival chip designer showed them that updates to the 6502 came out of what was effectively a one-person company, and they concluded they needed nothing more.
arm-one-person-company-1985.coda: ARM1 arrived on 26 April 1985 and worked on first power-up.

copyleft-all-rights-reversed.title: All Rights Reversed
copyleft-all-rights-reversed.body: Someone mailed Richard Stallman a letter marked "Copyleft — all rights reversed," a pun on the standard notice. After Symbolics enhanced his Lisp interpreter and declined to share the improvements back, he used copyright law itself to write a license demanding the opposite obligation.
copyleft-all-rights-reversed.coda: The General Public License followed in February 1989.

tetris-unpaid-decade.title: The Block With No Royalties
tetris-unpaid-decade.body: In 1985 Pajitnov wrote Tetris as a state employee of the USSR Academy of Sciences; the rights belonged to the Computing Center, not him. Western licenses passed through several hands before reaching Nintendo, and the game sold tens of millions of copies.
tetris-unpaid-decade.coda: The rights reverted to him in 1996, eleven years after he wrote it.

euv-twenty-three-hours-2018.title: Twenty-Three Hours for One Wafer
euv-twenty-three-hours-2018.body: Hiroo Kinoshita at NTT first demonstrated extreme ultraviolet lithography images in 1986. ASML's 2006 prototype took twenty-three hours to expose one wafer. Not until 2018 did EUV reach production, in a machine MIT Technology Review called the one that saved Moore's law.
euv-twenty-three-hours-2018.coda: By 2022 a production EUV scanner processed roughly two hundred wafers an hour.

tsmc-foundry-fifty-six-1987.title: A Foundry at Fifty-Six
tsmc-foundry-fifty-six-1987.body: Morris Chang, born 1931, rose to group vice president of worldwide semiconductor operations at Texas Instruments, then served as president and COO of General Instrument, then headed Taiwan's ITRI. In 1987, at fifty-six, he founded TSMC, which designs none of the chips it makes.
tsmc-foundry-fifty-six-1987.coda: It was the first foundry in the world to do nothing but manufacture.

huawei-diet-pills.title: Huawei's First Business Wasn't Tech
huawei-diet-pills.body: Huawei registered with 21,000 yuan of capital on September 15, 1987, calling itself a technology company. It began by trading goods, including diet pills, then resold Hong Kong-made HAX switches for the margin. Its own switch, the BH01, was hand-assembled only in 1989.
huawei-diet-pills.coda: Four years in, the company drew its own circuit board for the first time.

morris.title: A measurement
morris.body: Morris wanted to know how big the internet was, so he wrote a program that copied itself. To stop hosts faking an already-infected reply, he gave it a one-in-seven chance of reinfecting anyway.
morris.coda: That one-in-seven took down about 6,000 of the 60,000 hosts then online.

naur.title: The program is not the artifact
naur.body: Naur argued that a program does not live in its source but as a theory, held by the people who wrote it, of why the problem is solved this way. The source is a lossy projection of it.
naur.coda: He called the moment the last theory-holder leaves the death of the program.

mit-license-171-words.title: 171 Words
mit-license-171-words.body: A group at MIT writing a TCP/IP implementation wanted to avoid legal negotiation, so they gave the software away under a notice of roughly 171 words. That short text now covers close to a third of all licensed projects on GitHub, more than any other license.
mit-license-171-words.coda: The wording has stayed essentially unchanged since it was written.

photoshop-display-origin.title: It Was Called Display First
photoshop-display-origin.body: In 1988, Thomas Knoll, a graduate student at the University of Michigan, wrote a small program to view grayscale images on a monochrome Mac screen. He named it Display, then ImagePro, then Photoshop, before his brother John showed it to Adobe, which licensed it that year.
photoshop-display-origin.coda: Adobe bought full rights outright in 1995, for $34.5 million.

sosumi-so-sue-me.title: So Sue Me
sosumi-so-sue-me.body: In 1991, Apple's legal department rejected the alert-sound name "Let It Beep" as too musical, under a settlement barring Apple Computer from music-related trademarks. Sound designer Jim Reekes wrote back "so sue me," then filed it as "sosumi."
sosumi-so-sue-me.coda: The sound shipped in Mac OS for nearly three decades before Big Sur replaced it in 2020.

www-royalty-free.title: The day it stopped costing
www-royalty-free.body: On 30 April 1993 CERN made the protocol and the code of the World Wide Web available royalty-free. Anyone could take it, without paying and without asking.
www-royalty-free.coda: Nobody has paid a royalty to use it since.

doom-ftp-crash.title: The Server They Couldn't Reach
doom-ftp-crash.body: On 10 December 1993, id Software gave away Doom's first episode as shareware, betting on sales of the rest. Uploading it to a University of Wisconsin FTP server, they found so many people already waiting that the team itself could not connect.
doom-ftp-crash.coda: The upload finished near midnight; ten thousand downloads at once crashed the university's network.

zlib-two-authors.title: The Compression Layer of Two
zlib-two-authors.body: zlib sits inside Linux, macOS, iOS and successive generations of game consoles; Git and OpenSSH both lean on it to compress. Two people wrote its first public release in 1995.
zlib-two-authors.coda: The authorship line has never grown a third name.

byd-battery-to-car.title: The Battery Company Bought a Carmaker
byd-battery-to-car.body: BYD was founded in Shenzhen's Longgang district on February 10, 1995, making nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries, then entering lithium-ion cells in 1996. In 2003 the battery maker acquired Xi'an Qinchuan Automobile, renaming it BYD Auto.
byd-battery-to-car.coda: Two years later, its first in-house sedan, the F3, went on sale.

ariane-501.title: Thirty-seven seconds
ariane-501.body: Thirty-seven seconds in, the inertial reference system converted a 64-bit float to a 16-bit integer and overflowed; at about forty seconds the vehicle broke up. The routine came unchanged from Ariane 4 and had no reason to be running after liftoff.
ariane-501.coda: Roughly $370 million, spent on code that should have been switched off.

deep-blue-move-44-1997.title: Move Forty-Four's Glitch
deep-blue-move-44-1997.body: In game one of the 1997 rematch Kasparov beat Deep Blue in forty-five moves. Deep Blue's forty-fourth move was allegedly the result of a bug: unable to settle on a preferred move inside its search, the engine fell back to a fail-safe.
deep-blue-move-44-1997.coda: After losing game two, Kasparov accused IBM of cheating.

curl-one-maintainer.title: One Man's Protocol Stack
curl-one-maintainer.body: curl's own docs put libcurl on roughly ten billion devices, running on 110 operating systems and 28 CPU architectures. The project has carried Daniel Stenberg's name as lead maintainer since it was renamed curl in 1998.
curl-one-maintainer.coda: No named successor has ever been listed.

book-of-mozilla-verses.title: The Book of Mozilla
book-of-mozilla-verses.body: Typing about:mozilla into the address bar reveals the Book of Mozilla, an apocalyptic verse pitting 'the beast' against 'Mammon' that each browser generation updates. The verse numbers are not chapter markers: they are release dates.
book-of-mozilla-verses.coda: The newest verse, 6:27, first shipped in a Firefox Nightly build in 2020.

http-418-teapot.title: I'm a Teapot
http-418-teapot.body: RFC 2324, published April 1, 1998, defines status 418 as "I'm a teapot" and files itself as Informational, not a standard. On April 1, 2014, RFC 7168 extended it to cover tea brewing. The code still never became a real standard.
http-418-teapot.coda: Both documents remain Informational; the status code shipped in real servers anyway.

open-source-coined-1998.title: The Coining of Open Source
open-source-coined-1998.body: In February 1998, Christine Peterson proposed "open source" because newcomers kept hearing "free software" as a price, not a freedom. At a VA Research meeting on February 5, Todd Anderson slipped the term into conversation rather than formally proposing it, letting it spread on its own.
open-source-coined-1998.coda: The group later tried to trademark the phrase and failed.

netscape-source-1998.title: Not Quite Open
netscape-source-1998.body: On 22 January 1998 Netscape announced that its browser source would be released, and the employee Jamie Zawinski registered mozilla.org. But the licence they wrote kept one door open: Netscape itself could go on folding the same code into proprietary products.
netscape-source-1998.coda: Netscape was acquired by AOL roughly a year later.

bsd-75-acknowledgments.title: Seventy-Five Acknowledgments
bsd-75-acknowledgments.body: The original BSD license required every advertisement to credit each contributing author by name. By 1997 a single NetBSD build carried seventy-five such acknowledgments, incompatible with the GPL. Berkeley's licensing director deleted the clause on July 22, 1999.
bsd-75-acknowledgments.coda: One office's signature retired a clause that had multiplied for a decade.

red-hat-ipo-1999.title: The Price of Free Software
red-hat-ipo-1999.body: Red Hat gave away the source code of its core product and charged instead for support, training and integration. On August 11, 1999 the company went public. Its first-day gain ranked eighth-largest in Wall Street history at the time.
red-hat-ipo-1999.coda: Founder Bob Young was replaced as CEO four months later.

multics-shutdown.title: The last one
multics-shutdown.body: On 30 October 2000 the last known Multics installation running natively on Honeywell hardware was shut down at the Canadian Department of National Defence in Halifax, Nova Scotia.
multics-shutdown.coda: Thirty-five years after the project began.

sqlite-no-license.title: The Database With No License
sqlite-no-license.body: SQLite's own page estimates over a trillion active database files worldwide, since every smartphone alone carries hundreds, ranking it second only to zlib among deployed software. There is no license, because the authors gave every line to the public domain.
sqlite-no-license.coda: Companies wanting legal cover buy a separate warranty of title.

smic-tsmc-lawsuit.title: SMIC's Two Lawsuits
smic-tsmc-lawsuit.body: SMIC was founded in 2000 by Richard Chang, a former TSMC engineer, among others. TSMC sued twice for trade-secret theft; in the 2009 case a jury found SMIC liable on 61 of the 65 counts brought against it.
smic-tsmc-lawsuit.coda: In November 2010 SMIC settled with TSMC for $200 million and roughly 8 percent of its shares.

api-mandate.title: The memo
api-mandate.body: According to the post that went public by accident in 2011, Bezos ordered in 2002 that teams expose everything through service interfaces: no direct linking, no reading another team's store, no back doors.
api-mandate.coda: The author of that post had meant it for his colleagues only.

hupu-rumours.title: The one translating rumours
hupu-rumours.body: In January 2004 a Chinese student working on a mechanical engineering doctorate in Chicago started a basketball forum in his spare time. The work was mostly translating NBA news and rumours into Chinese and tidying them up.
hupu-rumours.coda: Eight years later the forum opened an online store of its own.

jd-the-other-name.title: The other half of the name
jd-the-other-name.body: The retail platform that went online in 2004 took its name from two people: its founder, Liu Qiangdong, and Gong Xiaojing, the woman he had dated first. One character from each.

douban-hutong.title: Named after the alley
douban-hutong.body: The site that went live on 6 March 2005 is not named after a metaphor. Yang Bo wrote its source in a cafe near Douban Hutong in Beijing, and took the name of the alley.
douban-hutong.coda: Twenty-one years on, the site still carries it.

git-information-manager-hell.title: Information Manager from Hell
git-information-manager-hell.body: On 7 April 2005 Linus Torvalds committed git's first revision. The message reads: Initial revision of "git", the information manager from hell. The author address on it is torvalds@ppc970.osdl.org.
git-information-manager-hell.coda: That address points to a PowerPC 970 test machine at OSDL.

knuth-reward-check.title: Bank of San Serriffe
knuth-reward-check.body: Donald Knuth pays $2.56 for each error found in his books, drawn on the fictional Bank of San Serriffe. By March 2005 the checks he had signed totaled over $20,000.
knuth-reward-check.coda: Most recipients frame the check rather than deposit it.

dji-helicopter-first.title: DJI Started With a Helicopter
dji-helicopter-first.body: Frank Wang graduated from Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in 2006 and co-founded DJI in Shenzhen with classmates. Its first product was a helicopter flight-control system; the first mature version, XP3.1, shipped in 2008.
dji-helicopter-first.coda: The team later found most gimbal buyers were mounting them on multirotors, not helicopters.

dropbox-hn.title: That reply
dropbox-hn.body: Houston posted the Dropbox demo to Hacker News. The famous reply explained that you could do it yourself with an FTP account, curlftpfs and SVN, and that it did not look like it would make money.
dropbox-hn.coda: Eleven years later, at the IPO, Houston called it his favourite thread on the site.

butterfield.title: Twice from the wreckage
butterfield.body: Butterfield's game, Game Neverending, stalled, and the team spun the photo-sharing piece out as Flickr. Eight years later his second game, Glitch, shut down, and the team spun out the chat tool they had built for themselves: Slack.
butterfield.coda: Both times the by-product only became visible once the main thing closed.

blockbuster.title: Fifty million
blockbuster.body: Hastings and Randolph flew to Dallas to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for fifty million, and to run the online side for them. By Randolph's account the CEO across the table spent the meeting suppressing a laugh.
blockbuster.coda: Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy ten years later.

y2k.title: Nothing happened
y2k.body: Gartner put the worldwide cost of Y2K at three to six hundred billion dollars, and hundreds of thousands of people changed two-digit years line by line. On the night, the grid held, the banks held, the planes flew.
y2k.coda: Four years later an economist published a paper arguing most of the money had been wasted.

unsourced.title: Attributed to nobody
unsourced.body: "640K ought to be enough for anybody" — Gates's own answer is that there is never a citation, that the quotation just floats like a rumour and gets repeated. "A world market for maybe five computers" — Thomas Watson did say five, in 1953, about the orders he expected for one machine, the IBM 701.
unsourced.coda: The 701 went on to sell eighteen.

homebrew-volunteer-team.title: The Repository With No Employer
homebrew-volunteer-team.body: Homebrew is the default package manager on most Mac developer machines; in 2013 it led all of GitHub in contributors. Max Howell wrote its first release in 2009. It is maintained today by a team of 34 people, all unpaid.
homebrew-volunteer-team.coda: Its funding history is one Kickstarter and an Open Source Collective account.

xiaomi-software-first.title: Xiaomi's First Product Wasn't a Phone
xiaomi-software-first.body: Xiaomi was founded on April 6, 2010. That August and December it released beta versions of the MIUI operating system and the Miliao chat app, both software.
xiaomi-software-first.coda: The company's first phone did not ship until August of the following year.

ritchie-same-week.title: Same Week
ritchie-same-week.body: Dennis Ritchie, with Ken Thompson, created Unix and the C programming language. He was found dead at his New Jersey home on October 12, 2011, at 70. Steve Jobs had died a week earlier, on October 5. Commentators later noted Ritchie's work underlay technology Apple built its fortune on.
ritchie-same-week.coda: The two obituaries ran in the same week.

leap-second.title: The extra second
leap-second.body: A leap second was inserted to keep atomic clocks in step with the earth's rotation. The kernel never told its timer subsystem, high-resolution timers fired early, and processors spun. Reddit, Mozilla and LinkedIn seized up; an airline boarded passengers by hand.
leap-second.coda: Time does not increase monotonically. Code assumes it does.

gregorian-1752-eleven-days.title: The Eleven Missing Days
gregorian-1752-eleven-days.body: On 2 September 1752, the British calendar jumped to 14 September, deleting eleven days. Popular history says mobs rioted over it. No contemporary record of any riot survives. The story traces to a banner in a 1755 satirical election painting.
gregorian-1752-eleven-days.coda: A prop from a painting became the record of an event with no other trace.

bootstrap-the-impossible-joke.title: Borrowed From an Impossible Feat
bootstrap-the-impossible-joke.body: "Pulling oneself up by one's bootstraps" traces to Baron Munchausen's 1785 tall tale and was used through the 19th century as the standard example of a physical impossibility. In 1953, computing borrowed it for the instruction chain that gets a machine to start itself.
bootstrap-the-impossible-joke.coda: The word for the trick was, on its first use, a punchline about the trick failing.

french-revolutionary-decimal-time.title: The Ten-Hour Day
french-revolutionary-decimal-time.body: In 1793 France divided the day into ten hours of a hundred decimal minutes each. Mandatory use began in September 1794 and was suspended just seven months later. The decimal face on the Tuileries Palace clock kept running at least through 1801.
french-revolutionary-decimal-time.coda: The abolished system stayed mounted on a palace wall for years afterward.

railway-time-gwr.title: The Time the Trains Kept
railway-time-gwr.body: In November 1840, the Great Western Railway adopted Greenwich time across its network, replacing each town's own local time. By 1855, about 98 percent of British towns had followed. Parliament did not make it the legal national standard until 1880.
railway-time-gwr.coda: The clocks agreed on the time forty years before the law did.

western-union-telephone-memo-1876.title: The Memo Western Union Never Wrote
western-union-telephone-memo-1876.body: A widely quoted 1876 Western Union memo calls the telephone "idiotic" next to sending a messenger to the telegraph office. Researchers combing period newspapers found no trace of it, and the executive it names did not hold that post at the company that year. The text was fabricated later.
western-union-telephone-memo-1876.coda: Western Union did decline Bell's patent that year; it just never wrote this memo.

nintendo-hanafuda-detours.title: The Detours After the Flower Cards
nintendo-hanafuda-detours.body: Fusajiro Yamauchi opened a shop in Kyoto in 1889 hand-making hanafuda playing cards. The company later tried a taxi service and instant rice, both abandoned; the widely repeated love-hotel chain claim has no record in securities filings researched back to 1962.
nintendo-hanafuda-detours.coda: In 1966 a toy called the Ultra Hand sold hundreds of thousands of units.

wrigley-premiums-premium.title: The Premium's Premium
wrigley-premiums-premium.body: In 1891 William Wrigley Jr. sold soap in Chicago and threw in baking powder as a bonus. Customers wanted the baking powder more than the soap, so he switched to selling that instead, and added chewing gum as baking powder's own bonus. Customers wanted the gum more.
wrigley-premiums-premium.coda: By 1892 he had dropped both soap and baking powder to sell only gum.

robot-labor-not-brother.title: Robot's Uncredited Coiner
robot-labor-not-brother.body: Karel Čapek drafted his 1920 play with a Latinate word, "laboři," and thought it too bookish. In a newspaper column he named the actual source: his brother Josef, tossed off in passing. "Robot" comes from robota — a serf's compulsory labor, not machinery.
robot-labor-not-brother.coda: The play kept one brother's name on the title page.

play-doh-wallpaper-cleaner.title: It Was Meant to Clean Wallpaper
play-doh-wallpaper-cleaner.body: In the 1930s, Kutol formulated a soft dough to scrub coal soot off wallpaper. Once homes switched to cleaner heating fuel, demand vanished. A teacher suggested selling it as modeling clay; it was renamed Play-Doh in 1956.
play-doh-wallpaper-cleaner.coda: By 2005 it was selling 95 million cans a year across 75 countries.

hedy-lamarr-frequency-hopping-patent.title: The Patent They Shelved
hedy-lamarr-frequency-hopping-patent.body: In 1942, Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented a frequency-hopping system to keep torpedo radio from being jammed. The Navy classified it, shelved it, and suggested Lamarr sell war bonds instead. The patent expired in 1959, before any ship carried it.
hedy-lamarr-frequency-hopping-patent.coda: Lamarr never received payment for the patent in her lifetime.

bush-1945-memex.title: The Desk Never Built
bush-1945-memex.body: In July 1945, Vannevar Bush published "As We May Think" in The Atlantic, describing a desk-sized microfilm machine called the Memex that let a user build associative trails through stored knowledge. It ran again in an abridged reprint that September. No prototype was ever built.
bush-1945-memex.coda: Engelbart and Nelson both later credited the essay as the reason they started.

jean-bartik-eniac-dinner.title: The Dinner They Weren't Invited To
jean-bartik-eniac-dinner.body: At ENIAC's public unveiling on February 14, 1946, the trajectory program that impressed the room had been written by Jean Bartik and Betty Holberton. The press introduced only Eckert and Mauchly. None of the six women programmers were invited to the dinner after.
jean-bartik-eniac-dinner.coda: Their names were pulled back out of the event photographs decades later.

claude-shannon-juggling-theorem.title: The Juggling Theorem
claude-shannon-juggling-theorem.body: In 1948, Shannon published 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication,' founding information theory. Decades later he turned the same rigor on his hobby, deriving a formal relationship between a ball's flight time, its dwell time, and the count of balls and hands.
claude-shannon-juggling-theorem.coda: It was collected in the same volume as the 1948 paper.

mccarthy-1960-eval.title: The Interpreter in the Footnote
mccarthy-1960-eval.body: In his 1960 paper, John McCarthy wrote an eval function as mathematical notation, to show that symbolic expressions could describe themselves. His student Steve Russell translated the derivation into IBM 704 machine code. The proof device became the first working Lisp interpreter.
mccarthy-1960-eval.coda: McCarthy later said he had not intended anyone to actually run it.

licklider-1960-symbiosis.title: Libraries Wired Together
licklider-1960-symbiosis.body: In his 1960 paper "Man-Computer Symbiosis," J.C.R. Licklider proposed "thinking centers" holding library functions, linked into a network for real-time, conversational use of computers. Most machines of the day ran on punch cards in batches; interactive terminals barely existed.
licklider-1960-symbiosis.coda: Two years later he ran a new Pentagon office and funded the project that became ARPANET.

ctss-1962-password-leak.title: The Password File, Printed
ctss-1962-password-leak.body: In 1962, MIT PhD student Allan Scherr was frustrated with his four hours a week on CTSS. He found the offline print command could pull any account's files, so he printed UACCNT.SECRET, the file holding every password, and shared it to borrow accounts and keep running his simulations.
ctss-1962-password-leak.coda: Scherr did not admit it to the lab's director until nearly thirty years later.

katherine-johnson-check-the-numbers.title: Have the Girl Check It
katherine-johnson-check-the-numbers.body: Before his 1962 orbital flight, John Glenn had engineers ask Katherine Johnson to hand-recompute the trajectory an IBM 7090 had already calculated. 'If she says they're good,' he said, 'I'm ready to go.' Her numbers matched the computer's exactly.

daemon-backronym.title: The Daemon's Retrofitted Acronym
daemon-backronym.body: In 1963, MIT's Project MAC programmers named a background tape-backup process after Maxwell's demon, an 1867 thought-experiment agent that sorts molecules tirelessly and invisibly — the Greek daimon, a neutral spirit, not the Judeo-Christian devil.
daemon-backronym.coda: "Disk And Execution MONitor" was fitted onto the word afterward.

sketchpad-1963.title: A Light Pen and an Oscilloscope
sketchpad-1963.body: In January 1963, Ivan Sutherland submitted his MIT thesis on Sketchpad, drawing constrained geometry with a light pen on the TX-2's screen at Lincoln Laboratory. The machine cost roughly a million dollars and only a handful existed; his drawing board could not be handed to anyone else.
sketchpad-1963.coda: Commercial CAD software took close to two decades to match what the thesis had shown.

douglas-mcilroy-garden-hose-pipe.title: The Garden Hose Memo
douglas-mcilroy-garden-hose-pipe.body: In October 1964, McIlroy wrote a Bell Labs memo proposing programs connect like garden hoses — screw in another segment to massage data differently. It circulated, was admired, and went unbuilt. Nine years later, Ken Thompson added one character, |, to the Unix shell overnight.
douglas-mcilroy-garden-hose-pipe.coda: By morning, programs that had never spoken to each other did.

berkshire-hathaway-spite-buy.title: The Mill Bought Out of Anger
berkshire-hathaway-spite-buy.body: In 1964 Warren Buffett verbally agreed to sell his shares back to Berkshire's president, Seabury Stanton, at $11.50 each. The written tender offer came in at $11.375. Buffett was angry enough over the missing eighth that he bought control of the company instead and fired Stanton.
berkshire-hathaway-spite-buy.coda: In 1985 he shut down the textile mills he had fought to keep.

nelson-1965-hypertext.title: The Link Before the Page
nelson-1965-hypertext.body: In a 1965 ACM paper, Ted Nelson coined "hypertext" for documents that link and quote each other non-sequentially, building on a project he had started in 1960 and later named Xanadu. His version paid original authors per link followed. A partial implementation did not ship until 2014.
nelson-1965-hypertext.coda: The Web adopted his vocabulary and left the payment mechanism behind.

mary-allen-wilkes-linc.title: The LINC in the Living Room
mary-allen-wilkes-linc.body: In 1965, Wilkes moved a 250-pound LINC computer into her parents' Baltimore living room and wrote LAP6, an interactive operating system, alone — twelve years before the Apple II reached any home. Asked if she was first, she said only: 'I guess I might have been.'
mary-allen-wilkes-linc.coda: She never claimed the title outright herself.

hoares-billion-dollar-mistake.title: The Reference He Added Anyway
hoares-billion-dollar-mistake.body: In 1965 Tony Hoare was building the first type system meant to make ALGOL W references provably safe at compile time. He added a null reference anyway, because it was easy to implement. In 2009 he called it his billion-dollar mistake.
hoares-billion-dollar-mistake.coda: The safety goal was explicit; the failure was that ease won anyway.

johnson-vs-cern-touchscreen.title: Who Actually Was First
johnson-vs-cern-touchscreen.body: CERN credits Bent Stumpe with building the world's first capacitive touchscreen in 1972, for its accelerator control room. Eric Johnson of Britain's Royal Radar Establishment had already published a paper on finger-driven capacitive touch technology in 1965, seven years earlier.
johnson-vs-cern-touchscreen.coda: CERN's claim to have built the first touchscreen still stands on its own website.

second-redefined-1967.title: 9,192,631,770 Cycles
second-redefined-1967.body: Until 1960, the second was a fraction of the 1900 tropical year, fixed by astronomical observation. In 1967 the General Conference on Weights and Measures redefined it as 9,192,631,770 cycles of a caesium-133 transition.
second-redefined-1967.coda: The length of a second stopped being set by the sun and started being set by an atom.

goto-statement-considered-harmful.title: The Title He Did Not Write
goto-statement-considered-harmful.body: Dijkstra submitted a paper titled A Case against the GO TO Statement to CACM. Editor Niklaus Wirth, rushing it into print as a letter, gave it the title that made it famous: Go To Statement Considered Harmful.
goto-statement-considered-harmful.coda: The phrase outran the letter, spawning decades of 'X Considered Harmful' titles nobody read past.

rollkugel-vs-mouse.title: Two Mice, One Year
rollkugel-vs-mouse.body: In October 1968, Telefunken listed the Rollkugel mouse in a sales brochure, a rolling-ball device its engineers had built since 1966. Two months later, on December 9, Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the wooden mouse his SRI team had built since 1963. Neither team knew of the other.
rollkugel-vs-mouse.coda: Telefunken reached the market first and was forgotten; Engelbart came second and is what people mean by mouse.

peter-principle-verified.title: Promoted to Incompetence
peter-principle-verified.body: In 1969, Laurence Peter and Raymond Hull half-joked in a bestseller that every employee rises to the level where they become incompetent, meant as satire. In 2019 a study of sales-force promotion data at 214 real firms found the joke held: top sellers made worse managers.
peter-principle-verified.coda: The punchline turned out to be a measurable, published regression coefficient.

lanpar-vs-visicalc.title: The Spreadsheet Nobody Named
lanpar-vs-visicalc.body: In summer 1969, Harvard graduates Rene Pardo and Remy Landau wrote LANPAR, a spreadsheet language that let users enter formulas in any order and still calculated correctly. Bell Canada and General Motors ran on it. In 1979, Dan Bricklin built VisiCalc without knowing LANPAR existed.
lanpar-vs-visicalc.coda: LANPAR's patent survived a court challenge through 1983; the magazines had already named VisiCalc first.

spam-vikings-not-marketers.title: Spam, Before Marketing
spam-vikings-not-marketers.body: In a 1970 sketch, Monty Python's Vikings chant "spam" over a diner's dialogue, mocking a glut of canned meat on the menu. The joke migrated into MUD chatrooms by the late 1980s for chat flooding, then onto email by the early 1990s.
spam-vikings-not-marketers.coda: The word reached inboxes by way of a comedy sketch about lunch.

codd-1970-relational-model.title: The Paper Its Employer Ignored
codd-1970-relational-model.body: In 1970, IBM researcher Edgar Codd published the relational model. IBM's flagship product was hierarchical, and the company was in no hurry to adopt his idea. Larry Ellison read Codd's paper and IBM's own System R reports, then shipped a commercial relational database first, in 1979.
codd-1970-relational-model.coda: IBM's own relational product, DB2, did not ship until 1983.

linnainmaa-backpropagation.title: The Missing Citation
linnainmaa-backpropagation.body: In 1970, Finnish student Seppo Linnainmaa published the complete algorithm for reverse-mode automatic differentiation, with working code, in his master's thesis. In 1986, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published the same method in Nature to train neural networks. They did not cite him.
linnainmaa-backpropagation.coda: Linnainmaa's thesis sat uncited for sixteen years before historians of the field dug it back up.

at-sign-arbitrary-pick.title: The Only Unused Key
at-sign-arbitrary-pick.body: In 1971, BBN engineer Ray Tomlinson needed a separator between username and host that could never appear in an actual person's name. Scanning his Model 33 Teletype keyboard, he picked @ — a character then used almost exclusively by grocers and bookkeepers.
at-sign-arbitrary-pick.coda: Every email address since has carried that one constraint forward.

parnas-module-decomposition.title: Where to Cut a Module
parnas-module-decomposition.body: In 1972 David Parnas split the same KWIC-index system into modules two ways: one by processing step, one by the design decisions most likely to change, each hidden behind an interface. Only the second let a change touch one module without anyone reading the rest.
parnas-module-decomposition.coda: The module boundary turned out to encode a guess about what a future maintainer would need to know.

karen-sparck-jones-idf.title: The Formula Nobody Thanks
karen-sparck-jones-idf.body: In 1972, Spärck Jones published a paper proposing that a word's rarity across a document collection measures its importance — inverse document frequency, now under the ranking logic of nearly every search engine. She got no permanent post at Cambridge until 1993.
karen-sparck-jones-idf.coda: Until then she had worked a run of short-term, soft-money contracts.

cyclades-pouzin-tcpip.title: The Internet's Fifth Man
cyclades-pouzin-tcpip.body: In 1972, Louis Pouzin built the CYCLADES network in France, the first to make end hosts, not the network, responsible for reliable delivery. In 1974, Cerf and Kahn's TCP paper thanked him by name. In 2004, Cerf and Kahn won the Turing Award. Pouzin's name was not on it.
cyclades-pouzin-tcpip.coda: The Economist later called him the internet's fifth man.

ethernet-1973-memo.title: The Ether Memo
ethernet-1973-memo.body: On May 22, 1973, Robert Metcalfe wrote a Xerox PARC memo titled "Ether Acquisition," with a hand-drawn diagram of a shared cable linking Alto computers. The technology is usually dated to the 1976 journal paper. The actual sketch is three years older, and hand-drawn.
ethernet-1973-memo.coda: By the time the paper was published, Ethernet had already run inside PARC for three years.

vint-cerf-envelope-sketch.title: The Back of an Envelope
vint-cerf-envelope-sketch.body: The internet's founding legend says Cerf sketched the gateway architecture on a napkin. He has corrected this: 'It wasn't a napkin, actually, it was the back of an envelope.' In 1973, waiting in a hotel lobby, he sketched what became TCP/IP's gateway design.
vint-cerf-envelope-sketch.coda: The following year, the sketch became a paper in IEEE Transactions on Communications.

gchq-nonsecret-encryption.title: The Unpublished Key
gchq-nonsecret-encryption.body: In September 1973, 22-year-old Clifford Cocks, newly arrived at GCHQ, worked out a shared-key-free encryption scheme in half an hour. Three years later, Diffie, Hellman and Merkle published the same idea in the US and were credited as its inventors. GCHQ files stayed classified until 1997.
gchq-nonsecret-encryption.coda: James Ellis died in 1997, a few months after the declassification that put his name on the record.

kodak-digital-camera-1975.title: Kodak's Buried Camera
kodak-digital-camera-1975.body: In 1975, 24-year-old engineer Steven Sasson built the first digital camera: 8 pounds, 23 seconds per shot. Executives reasoned that no one would want to view pictures on a television when print was cheap and had worked for a century. They patented the camera and shelved it.
kodak-digital-camera-1975.coda: Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012.

galls-law-origin.title: A Book About Bureaucracies
galls-law-origin.body: In 1975, after 30 publishers rejected it, pediatrician John Gall self-published Systemantics: a working complex system invariably evolves from a working simple system, and a complex system built from scratch never works. He was writing about hospitals and government agencies.
galls-law-origin.coda: Software architects kept the line and quietly dropped the bureaucracies it was written about.

ken-olsen-home-computer-1977.title: Olsen's Home Computer
ken-olsen-home-computer-1977.body: In 1977, DEC founder Ken Olsen said there was no reason for an individual to have a computer in the home. He meant one central machine running the lights, heat and entertainment for a household, accurate for the thing he described. Coverage kept only the first half of the sentence.
ken-olsen-home-computer-1977.coda: Olsen himself owned a computer at home at the time.

kernighans-debugging-law.title: Twice as Hard as Writing It
kernighans-debugging-law.body: In the 1978 Elements of Programming Style, Kernighan and Plauger wrote that debugging is twice as hard as writing a program, so writing it as cleverly as you can leaves you, by definition, not smart enough to debug it. A style rule stated as a limit on meeting your own work twice.
kernighans-debugging-law.coda: The adversary was never someone else, it was you a few weeks later.

xerox-parc-1979-visit.title: Xerox's Own Deal
xerox-parc-1979-visit.body: December 1979: Apple toured Xerox PARC after Xerox agreed to buy 100,000 pre-IPO Apple shares at $10 each for the access. Jobs saw the Alto's graphical interface and called it the best thing he'd ever seen. The popular story is theft; the record is a trade Xerox negotiated.
xerox-parc-1979-visit.coda: Xerox got its shares. The Alto was never sold as a commercial product.

visicalc-1979-no-patent.title: The Patent They Skipped
visicalc-1979-no-patent.body: Before VisiCalc's 1979 release, Dan Bricklin consulted a patent attorney, who put the odds of success at about one in ten under the era's rules. They filed for copyright and trademark instead. In 1983, Lotus 1-2-3 shipped a compatible interface that could read VisiCalc's own files.
visicalc-1979-no-patent.coda: The spreadsheet survived as a category. The company that built it did not.

ibm-microsoft-dos-1980.title: IBM Leaves a Door Open
ibm-microsoft-dos-1980.body: IBM signed with Microsoft on the PC's operating system on November 6, 1980. Deep in a decade-plus antitrust case, IBM chose not to control its suppliers, and let Microsoft resell DOS to anyone else. As a hedge against another lawsuit, it made sense at the time.
ibm-microsoft-dos-1980.coda: Clone makers followed within years, and IBM never regained control of the platform.

postel-law-robustness-reversal.title: The Robustness Principle, Reversed
postel-law-robustness-reversal.body: RFC 761 (1980) urged implementers to be liberal in what they accept, conservative in what they send. In 2023 the IETF's own architecture board reversed that guidance in RFC 9413: leniency lets bugs calcify into de facto standards, leaving systems less robust, not more.
postel-law-robustness-reversal.coda: The standard that told the internet to be lenient was rescinded by its own custodians.

end-to-end-argument.title: An Argument for a Dumb Network
end-to-end-argument.body: In 1981 Saltzer, Reed, and Clark argued that checking a transferred file for errors can only be done correctly at the two endpoints; the network can help but never fully substitute. A paper about where to put a checksum became the founding case for keeping networks simple.
end-to-end-argument.coda: A note on error-checking placement grew into the case for net neutrality.

excel-1900-leap-year.title: The Leap Year That Wasn't
excel-1900-leap-year.body: Lotus 1-2-3 treated 1900 as a leap year, a harmless shortcut. Microsoft copied the same false date to stay compatible. Lotus is gone; the false leap day remains, now written into the Office Open XML specification.
excel-1900-leap-year.coda: A compatibility hack for a discontinued rival is now a written standard.

avatar-before-snow-crash.title: An Avatar Before the Novel
avatar-before-snow-crash.body: Neal Stephenson's 1992 novel Snow Crash is usually credited with the online sense of "avatar." But Lucasfilm's Habitat, running on Commodore 64s since 1985, already wrote: "players are represented by animated figures that we call Avatars," from Sanskrit for incarnation.
avatar-before-snow-crash.coda: The term was live on a commercial service seven years before the book.

radia-perlman-algorhyme.title: Algorhyme
radia-perlman-algorhyme.body: In 1985, Perlman's manager at DEC assigned the loop-free bridging problem on a Friday, then vanished for a week. She had the spanning-tree algorithm finished by Wednesday — and spent the rest writing Algorhyme, a poem that became the paper's abstract.
radia-perlman-algorhyme.coda: The poem took longer to write than the algorithm.

brooks-no-silver-bullet.title: No Silver Bullet
brooks-no-silver-bullet.body: At the 1986 IFIP congress, Fred Brooks split software difficulty into essential and accidental complexity. Accidental difficulty had fallen sharply, he said, but no single technique would deliver a tenfold productivity gain within a decade.
brooks-no-silver-bullet.coda: Four decades on, each new paradigm still gets sold as the bullet he said did not exist.

tz-olson-database.title: The Olson Database
tz-olson-database.body: Most devices resolve timezones against one volunteer-run file set, informally called the Olson database after founder Arthur David Olson. Its naming scheme is credited to Paul Eggert, who has actually edited the database since 2005.
tz-olson-database.coda: The eponym and the person who has maintained it since are different people.

china-1987-first-email.title: Beyond the Wall
china-1987-first-email.body: Retellings credit Qian Tianbai alone with China's first email, 'Across the Great Wall we can reach every corner of the world.' Qian was studying in the US that month; it was typed by Li Chengjiong and Karlsruhe's Werner Zorn, and left China six days later, on September 20.
china-1987-first-email.coda: His obituaries still list him as the sender.

barbara-liskov-substitution-property.title: The Law She Never Named
barbara-liskov-substitution-property.body: In a 1987 OOPSLA keynote, Barbara Liskov proposed that if substituting an object of type S for type T left every program's behavior unchanged, S was a subtype of T. She called it a substitution property. Years later, Robert Martin folded it into SOLID and named it after her.
barbara-liskov-substitution-property.coda: The word 'principle' was someone else's addition.

go-corporation-pen-computing.title: The Tablet Nobody Bought
go-corporation-pen-computing.body: In 1987 Jerry Kaplan started GO Corporation to build the pen-based PenPoint operating system, raising $75 million. AT&T acquired GO in January 1994, cancelled its supporting chip line two weeks later, and GO closed that July. Kaplan later said the company had "no meaningful sales."
go-corporation-pen-computing.coda: In 2010 Apple released the iPad, a capacitive multitouch tablet.

iso8601-unify-then-fork.title: ISO 8601's Narrower Stand-in
iso8601-unify-then-fork.body: ISO 8601 was first published in 1988, unifying five earlier, conflicting ISO date-and-time standards into one. But the format most internet software validates against is RFC 3339 (1997), a narrower profile that, after ISO 8601's later revision, is not even a strict subset of it.
iso8601-unify-then-fork.coda: The standard everyone cites and the dialect everyone's code checks against are not the same document.

python-christmas-project.title: A Christmas Hobby
python-christmas-project.body: During the Christmas holidays of 1989, with his office closed for the week, a researcher in Amsterdam looked for a hobby programming project. He began writing an interpreter for a new scripting language and named it after a comedy troupe, not the snake.
python-christmas-project.coda: In July 2026 it ranked first on the TIOBE index of programming language popularity.

worse-is-better.title: Worse Is Better
worse-is-better.body: In 1989 Richard Gabriel coined 'worse is better': a simple, half-right implementation survives better than a complete, correct one, which is why he thought C and Unix beat Lisp. In 1991 he published a rebuttal under the pseudonym Nickieben Bourbaki, posing as an old friend.
worse-is-better.coda: Decades later he still said he could not decide whether his own argument was right.

rfc1149-avian-carriers-test.title: The Protocol Someone Actually Flew
rfc1149-avian-carriers-test.body: David Waitzman published RFC 1149 on April Fools' Day, 1990: a spec for carrying IP datagrams by pigeon. On April 28, 2001, the Bergen Linux User Group actually built it, launching nine ping packets over roughly 5 km. Four came back — a 55% loss rate, round trips running 53 to 106 minutes.
rfc1149-avian-carriers-test.coda: The joke RFC has a real packet-loss figure on record: 55 percent.

att-1990-break-statement.title: The Misplaced Break
att-1990-break-statement.body: A recovery routine on a New York 4ESS switch held a break statement nested one level too shallow, a defect testing never exercised. A restart's routine "ready" signal was then misread by neighboring switches as an error, and the false alarm cascaded through the network for nine hours.
att-1990-break-statement.coda: AT&T later put the lost revenue at sixty million dollars.

aspec-vs-musicam.title: Losing to the Simpler One
aspec-vs-musicam.body: In 1991, MPEG tested two rival audio codecs. ASPEC, built by Fraunhofer, AT&T and France's CNET, won the quality tests but was ruled too complex. MUSICAM, from Matsushita and Philips, won on simplicity. The finished MP3 folded ASPEC's filter design back in anyway.
aspec-vs-musicam.coda: The format everyone calls MP3 carries the losing proposal's engineering inside the winning one's name.

linux-minix-post.title: A Post to comp.os.minix
linux-minix-post.body: On August 25, 1991, a Helsinki university student posted to the comp.os.minix newsgroup that he was writing a free operating system, calling it "just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu," and asked what features people wanted.
linux-minix-post.coda: Since November 2017, all 500 of the world's fastest supercomputers have run an OS built on it.

web-vs-gopher-1991.title: Free Beat Priced
web-vs-gopher-1991.body: In 1991, Tim Berners-Lee released the World Wide Web from CERN. That same year, the University of Minnesota released Gopher, for a time the more popular system. In February 1993, Minnesota announced licensing fees for Gopher servers. That April, CERN made the web protocol free.
web-vs-gopher-1991.coda: Gopher had the bigger following before the fee announcement, and never had it again afterward.

rough-consensus-running-code.title: Rough Consensus, Running Code
rough-consensus-running-code.body: At the July 1992 IETF meeting, MIT's Dave Clark put up a slide: 'We reject kings, presidents and voting. We believe in rough consensus and running code.' The phrase now anchors internet-governance folklore. It began as a jab at OSI's formal committee voting process.
rough-consensus-running-code.coda: The joke slide about OSI's voting rules became internet governance's founding creed.

han-unification-japanese-delegate.title: Han Unification's Unlikely Author
han-unification-japanese-delegate.body: In 1992 the CJK Joint Research Group merged tens of thousands of Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters into shared Unicode code points. Popular retellings cast Japan as the objector. Unicode's own history credits the verification rules to Japanese delegate Miyazawa Akira.
han-unification-japanese-delegate.coda: The delegation cast as the victim helped write the rules it is remembered for opposing.

china-first-internet-line.title: The Line a Year Early
china-first-internet-line.body: China marks April 20, 1994 as the day it joined the global internet — a 64K line, full-function access. Thirteen months earlier, physicists at IHEP had already leased a line to Stanford's SLAC, exchanging email with dozens of institutions. It just wasn't the kind of line anyone counted.
china-first-internet-line.coda: Two lines exist; only one gets an anniversary.

wiki-the-airport-shuttle.title: Named After a Shuttle Bus
wiki-the-airport-shuttle.body: "Wiki" is Hawaiian for "quick." In 1995, Ward Cunningham needed a name for the first editable web system he built and reached not for any technical term but for his memory of the Wiki Wiki Shuttle, the free bus between terminals at Honolulu's airport.
wiki-the-airport-shuttle.coda: The word's first home was painted on the side of an airport bus.

robots-exclusion-rfc9309.title: robots.txt: 28 Years Unratified
robots-exclusion-rfc9309.body: Martijn Koster proposed robots.txt in 1994; crawlers followed it voluntarily, with no formal standard and nothing to enforce it. Google proposed standardization in 2019, and the IETF finally published RFC 9309 in September 2022, closing a 28-year gap.
robots-exclusion-rfc9309.coda: The web's most-obeyed gentleman's agreement took twenty-eight years to become a real standard.

pentium-fdiv-writeoff.title: The Missing Table Entries
pentium-fdiv-writeoff.body: Mathematician Thomas Nicely noticed his new Pentium returning slightly wrong results while summing reciprocals of primes, and traced the fault to the chip itself. Intel first offered replacements only to customers who complained, and reversed into a full recall only under public pressure.
pentium-fdiv-writeoff.coda: Intel booked a $475 million pretax charge for the recall.

general-magic-private-network.title: General Magic's Private Wire
general-magic-private-network.body: In 1990 ex-Apple engineers Bill Atkinson, Andy Hertzfeld and Marc Porat founded General Magic. Sony's Magic Link shipped in 1994 for $800, sending email and running apps. Leadership built a proprietary AT&T network instead of using the internet, calling the web "passive."
general-magic-private-network.coda: Employee Tony Fadell later led hardware development on the iPod and iPhone at Apple.

ibm-simon-first-touchscreen.title: Simon's Fax Machine
ibm-simon-first-touchscreen.body: On August 16, 1994, IBM and BellSouth launched the Simon Personal Communicator: a 4.5-inch touchscreen that sent email and fax, priced at $899. Battery life ran about an hour. It was discontinued six months later, having sold roughly 50,000 units.
ibm-simon-first-touchscreen.coda: In 2007 Apple shipped the iPhone, a capacitive touchscreen phone with no physical keyboard.

cors-same-origin-orphaned.title: CORS: A Recommendation in Retirement
cors-same-origin-orphaned.body: Netscape bolted the same-origin policy onto Navigator in 1995, alongside JavaScript, with no standards process at all. CORS, meant to formally relax that policy, only became a W3C Recommendation in 2014 — and by 2020 the W3C had retired it, handing the spec to WHATWG's Fetch document.
cors-same-origin-orphaned.coda: The standards body retired its own security recommendation six years after publishing it.

php-resume-counter.title: A Résumé Hit Counter
php-resume-counter.body: In 1994, a programmer wrote a handful of small CGI programs in C for no larger reason than wanting to know how many people were looking at his online résumé. He called the toolkit "Personal Home Page Tools" and released the source in June 1995.
php-resume-counter.coda: Three decades on, over 70% of websites with a known server-side language still run its descendant.

craigslist-email-list.title: A Mailing List of Events
craigslist-email-list.body: In 1995, a software engineer in San Francisco started compiling the local gatherings and events he knew about into an email and sending it to a few friends, mainly so people could get to know one another a little better.
craigslist-email-list.coda: The list now reaches 570 cities in 70 countries and draws over 140 million visits a month.

wirths-law-misattributed.title: The Law He Credited Away
wirths-law-misattributed.body: In 1995 Niklaus Wirth published 'A Plea for Lean Software,' writing that software is getting slower more rapidly than hardware is getting faster. The line later christened Wirth's Law was, by his own footnote, a quotation of his colleague Martin Reiser.
wirths-law-misattributed.coda: The eponym cited the source; posterity kept only the eponym.

general-magic-weekend-site.title: The Site He Wasn't Serious About
general-magic-weekend-site.body: In the mid-1990s, at a Silicon Valley startup expected to reinvent handheld computing, one programmer spent his spare time writing a scrappy little site for selling secondhand junk. It went up on a weekend. He wasn't taking it seriously.
general-magic-weekend-site.coda: The startup was General Magic. The site was later renamed eBay.

gettickcount-776-day-bug.title: A 776-Day Debt
gettickcount-776-day-bug.body: Windows 95's GetTickCount rolls to zero every 49.7 days, documented behavior, never treated as a bug. But on Windows 8 through Server 2019, the same function could roll over early, near 776 days, a genuine defect. Microsoft fixed it only in Windows 11, version 24H2.
gettickcount-776-day-bug.coda: The fix landed three decades after the counter it patches first shipped.

bluetooth-the-placeholder.title: The Codename That Stuck
bluetooth-the-placeholder.body: In 1996, Intel's Jim Kardach proposed "Bluetooth" — after Harald Bluetooth, the Viking king who united Scandinavia — as a throwaway codename during Ericsson-Nokia talks. The intended replacement, RadioWire, could not clear trademark search before launch.
bluetooth-the-placeholder.coda: No replacement name ever made it to market.

chinaren-detour.title: The Off-Roster Coder
chinaren-detour.body: In 1996 a Chinese student won gold at the Informatics Olympiad and was admitted straight into Tsinghua's computer science program. As a student he moonlighted building a content system for an alumnus's website. Sohu bought it the next year; he stayed on and kept working there.
chinaren-detour.coda: The student was Wang Xiaochuan. In 2004, inside Sohu, he built Sogou.

google-a-typo.title: A Misspelled Domain Search
google-a-typo.body: During a September 1997 brainstorm, Sean Anderson suggested "googolplex"; Larry Page shortened it to "googol." Checking the domain registry on the spot, Anderson typed "google" by mistake and found it unclaimed. Page registered google.com that same day.
google-a-typo.coda: The registration record still carries the misspelling, dated September 15, 1997.

rfc2119-must-should.title: MUST vs must: A Twenty-Year Gap
rfc2119-must-should.body: RFC 2119 (March 1997) defined MUST, SHOULD, MAY and their negatives as binding requirement levels for IETF documents. But it only said these words 'are often capitalized' — lowercase must and should were never excluded. RFC 8174 patched the loophole in 2017: only all-caps counts.
rfc2119-must-should.coda: For twenty years, a lowercase must carried the same legal weight as a shrug.

netease-license-mail-1997.title: Sell the license first
netease-license-mail-1997.body: On June 11, 1997, William Ding registered NetEase in Guangzhou. The company's first business was not free webmail. It licensed a piece of email server software it had built to other websites for a fee.
netease-license-mail-1997.coda: NetEase did not launch its own free email, under 163.com, until 1998.

lixiang-graphics-card-home.title: Graphics Card Home
lixiang-graphics-card-home.body: In 1998, a high school student in Hebei started a personal website called Graphics Card Home in his spare time, posting reviews of computer graphics cards. Two years later he renamed it PCPop and kept updating it through the rest of school.
lixiang-graphics-card-home.coda: In 2005 the same person founded Autohome.

china-oicq-to-qq.title: From OICQ to QQ
china-oicq-to-qq.body: Tencent launched OICQ in February 1999 — the O stood for 'Open,' a nod to ICQ. That October, AOL, ICQ's owner, sent a cease-and-desist over trademark infringement. In November 2000, Ma Huateng renamed it QQ, chosen because the letter reads as 'cute' in Chinese.
china-oicq-to-qq.coda: Open was the first word to go once AOL's lawyers arrived.

excite-google-1999.title: Excite Turns Down Google
excite-google-1999.body: In 1999 Google offered to sell itself to Excite for $750,000 plus roughly 1% equity. CEO George Bell judged the search gap too small to justify tearing out Excite's technology. The reasoning held up. Google was worth over a billion within a year.
excite-google-1999.coda: Bell has said since that he would make the same call again.

mars-climate-orbiter-units.title: Pound-Force, Newton
mars-climate-orbiter-units.body: Mars Climate Orbiter went silent during orbital insertion. The board found that the contractor's thruster software output impulse in pound-force seconds while navigation software expected newton-seconds, off by a factor of 4.45. The craft was steered to within roughly 57 km of the surface.
mars-climate-orbiter-units.coda: The $327.6 million mission never transmitted again.

paypal-palm-beaming.title: The Beam That Never Came
paypal-palm-beaming.body: In 1999 Confinity launched infrared cash transfers between Palm Pilots, demoed live at a funding event. Weeks after launch it had roughly 13,000 users, a number that barely moved over the following year. What actually took off was email payments, built only as a fallback option.
paypal-palm-beaming.coda: The company renamed itself PayPal and quietly dropped the beam.

cai-500-yuan.title: The 500-Yuan Salary
cai-500-yuan.body: In 1999 a Hong Kong investment executive traveled to Hangzhou to assess a small website as a possible investment. He found a dozen-odd people coding in one crowded apartment. He didn't invest — he quit his $700,000 salary and joined instead, for 500 yuan a month.
cai-500-yuan.coda: His name was Joe Tsai. He later became Alibaba's executive vice chairman.

gps-week-rollover.title: GPS Week 1024
gps-week-rollover.body: GPS counts weeks in 10 bits, a field that maxes at 1,023 and rolls to zero roughly every 19.7 years. The first rollover hit in August 1999. The second landed on 6 April 2019, breaking receivers built as if the first had been a one-off.
gps-week-rollover.coda: The same overflow is on a schedule and due to recur again in 2038.

foxmail-resold.title: Sold With the Software
foxmail-resold.body: In 1994 a programmer in Guangzhou wrote a free email client in his spare time. In 2000, as the dot-com bubble burst, he sold it to a company and stayed on as tech director. Five years later that company folded and sold the software — and him with it — to Tencent.
foxmail-resold.coda: The programmer was Zhang Xiaolong. Five years after that, inside Tencent, he built WeChat.

danger-duarte-android-reunion.title: Design Director, Failed Startup
danger-duarte-android-reunion.body: In 2000 a designer joined a handheld-device startup founded by Andy Rubin, working on its interface. The company was sold to Microsoft and the team scattered. The designer went on to two other companies over the next decade.
danger-duarte-android-reunion.coda: The designer was Matias Duarte. Ten years later Rubin hired him onto Android.

slashdot-ipod-2001.title: No Wireless, Less Space
slashdot-ipod-2001.body: When Apple unveiled the first iPod on October 23, 2001, Slashdot founder Rob "CmdrTaco" Malda wrote in his editor's note: "No wireless. Less space than a nomad. Lame." Against the spec sheets of rival MP3 players at the time, the line was not factually wrong.
slashdot-ipod-2001.coda: The comment is now cited routinely as the counterexample it produced.

discuz-shenyang-dorm.title: CDB, a dorm build
discuz-shenyang-dorm.body: In 2001, a university student living in a dormitory in Shenyang wrote a piece of forum software and named it Crossday Bulletin, working on it alongside his coursework. The following October he renamed it Discuz.
discuz-shenyang-dorm.coda: On August 23, 2010, Tencent acquired the company he had built around it.

wikipedia-side-wiki.title: A Side Project Next to Nupedia
wikipedia-side-wiki.body: On January 10, 2001, the founder of a peer-reviewed online encyclopedia installed wiki software on the project's own server, mainly so volunteers could try drafting entries loosely on the side while the reviewed encyclopedia moved slowly ahead.
wikipedia-side-wiki.coda: By July 2026 its English edition alone held over 7.2 million articles.

bittorrent-mailing-list.title: A New P2P App
bittorrent-mailing-list.body: On July 2, 2001, a programmer posted a message to a Yahoo eGroups mailing list titled "BitTorrent -- a new P2P app," describing a file-distribution protocol he had just finished designing, one that pulled pieces of a file from many sources at once.
bittorrent-mailing-list.coda: Three years later it accounted for a third of all internet traffic, per a 2004 CacheLogic study.

webvan-thirty-minute-window.title: The Thirty-Minute Window
webvan-thirty-minute-window.body: In 1996 Borders bookstore co-founder Louis Borders started Webvan, promising 30-minute delivery on warehouses built from scratch. It IPO'd in November 1999 for $375 million at a valuation over $4.8 billion, then filed for bankruptcy in July 2001, having lost more than $800 million.
webvan-thirty-minute-window.coda: Some Webvan executives went on to Amazon; Amazon Fresh and Instacart later filled the same order.

kozmo-free-hour-delivery.title: The Free-Hour Promise
kozmo-free-hour-delivery.body: In 1998 Joseph Park and Yong Kang founded Kozmo.com, promising free one-hour delivery with couriers dispatched by pager. It raised roughly $250 million but earned $3.5 million against a $26.3 million loss in 1999. In April 2001, staff learned of the shutdown by finding closed offices.
kozmo-free-hour-delivery.coda: DoorDash, founded in 2013, dispatches couriers by smartphone GPS and charges a delivery fee.

flooz-digital-currency.title: Money With No Store
flooz-digital-currency.body: In February 1999, iVillage co-founder Robert Levitan launched Flooz.com, a digital currency users could buy and spend at partner merchants. A crime ring used stolen cards to mint $300,000 in fraudulent credits, and by 2001 fraud reached 19% of volume. The company folded that August.
flooz-digital-currency.coda: In January 2009, Satoshi Nakamoto mined bitcoin's genesis block.

yahoo-google-2002.title: Yahoo Passes on Google
yahoo-google-2002.body: In 2002 Yahoo CEO Terry Semel offered $3 billion for Google; Page and Brin held out for $5 billion. Semel's read was that Yahoo's own market cap, near $5 billion after the crash, could not absorb that bet. Google went public two years later at $23 billion.
yahoo-google-2002.coda: Yahoo sold its core business to Verizon in 2017 for $4.48 billion.

pplive-dorm-2002.title: Building 26, Yunyuan
pplive-dorm-2002.body: During the 2002 World Cup, Yao Xin's dorm at Huazhong University of Science and Technology had no television, so he watched matches over the campus network, which kept crashing. In his room in Building 26 he started working out how to combine peer-to-peer transfer with streaming video.
pplive-dorm-2002.coda: PPLive launched in 2005 and, at its peak, counted over a hundred million users.

china-alipay-escrow.title: The Escrow Workaround
china-alipay-escrow.body: In 2003, with Taobao buyers and sellers unwilling to trust each other first, finance built an escrow workaround: payment sat frozen until goods were confirmed. The first trade closed that October — a student in Xi'an paying a seller in Japan. The name puns 'pay' and 'guarantee.'
china-alipay-escrow.coda: The pun became the company's permanent, official name.

china-taobao-free-vs-ebay.title: Three Years Free
china-taobao-free-vs-ebay.body: In 2003, eBay's Eachnet held over 70 percent of China's C2C market, charging listing and transaction fees. Taobao launched that May to a near-empty site; Alibaba's answer was three years of free listings. By 2006, Taobao held 70 percent and eBay withdrew from Chinese C2C.
china-taobao-free-vs-ebay.coda: The side still charging listing fees ran out of runway first.

dianping-zagat-notes.title: A Zagat notebook
dianping-zagat-notes.body: In 2002, Zhang Tao came back to China from the United States carrying an idea he had picked up there: the Zagat Survey, a restaurant guide built from readers' own ratings. He registered the domain zsurvey.com and set out to build a Chinese version in Shanghai.
dianping-zagat-notes.coda: Dianping, the site that grew from it, went live on April 12, 2003.

wordpress-b2-post.title: The Blogging Software Dilemma
wordpress-b2-post.body: On January 24, 2003, a university student wrote on his own blog that b2, the blogging software he used daily, had gone unmaintained for months since its lead developer disappeared. He said he wanted to fork it and asked only for a name.
wordpress-b2-post.coda: The company that grew out of that fork was valued at $7.5 billion by 2021.

2003-blackout-race-condition.title: The Alarm That Didn't Ring
2003-blackout-race-condition.body: The alarm process at an Ohio control room silently jammed: a coding error let two processes gain write access to the same data structure at once, looping forever. Operators never saw the overload warnings and failed to shed load in time. The cascade left 55 million people without power.
2003-blackout-race-condition.coda: Engineers needed eight weeks to reproduce the race condition.

aws-not-leftover-servers.title: Not the Leftover Servers
aws-not-leftover-servers.body: The common version says AWS began by reselling Amazon's idle holiday-season server capacity. Benjamin Black calls that flatly false: in 2003 he and Chris Pinkham wrote a memo proposing standardized, automated infrastructure, purpose-built from the start to be sold externally as a service.
aws-not-leftover-servers.coda: S3 and EC2 launched in 2006, following that memo.

maps-intern-friendfeed.title: The Maps Team Intern
maps-intern-friendfeed.body: In 2003 a Google product manager hired an intern onto the team building local search, the project that grew into Google Maps. Four years later that intern and an engineer who had built Gmail left Google together to start a company.
maps-intern-friendfeed.coda: The intern was Bret Taylor. The company he left to start was bought by Facebook.

friendster-forty-second-load.title: The Forty-Second Load
friendster-forty-second-load.body: Friendster launched in 2002 and reached over 100 million registered accounts, but its servers buckled under the load of computing degrees of connection between friends; a single page could take forty seconds to load. Support emails show users threatening to defect to the newer MySpace.
friendster-forty-second-load.coda: Facebook launched in 2004 on the same social-graph idea and held under the traffic.

shopify-snowdevil-software.title: The Store Software Outgrew the Store
shopify-snowdevil-software.body: In 2004, programmer Tobias Lutke found the e-commerce software of the day too clunky, so he wrote his own to sell snowboard gear online as Snowdevil. Snowdevil itself stayed a small shop, but other merchants started asking to license the software behind it.
shopify-snowdevil-software.coda: Shopify listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2015.

twitter-odeo-podcast-pivot.title: The Podcast Company's Side Project
twitter-odeo-podcast-pivot.body: On June 28, 2005, Apple built podcast subscriptions into iTunes; within two days subscriptions passed one million, and Odeo's entire podcasting business went obsolete overnight. The next March, an internal hackathon produced Jack Dorsey's SMS status-update pitch: Twitter.
twitter-odeo-podcast-pivot.coda: Odeo, the company Twitter was built inside, was sold off in 2007.

youtube-tune-in-hook-up.title: The Domain Registered on Valentine's Day
youtube-tune-in-hook-up.body: youtube.com was registered on February 14, 2005, and its founders later told of a dating-site concept modeled on Hot or Not. Jawed Karim denied attending the dinner party the story hinges on, and Steve Chen conceded it reads like a marketing narrative.
youtube-tune-in-hook-up.coda: What Karim cited instead was trouble finding tsunami footage online.

duan-buffett-lunch.title: The Buffett Lunch
duan-buffett-lunch.body: In 2006 a Guangdong electronics manufacturer won the annual charity auction for lunch with Warren Buffett, paying $620,100. He brought along a 26-year-old who had just quit an American company and had no clear plan yet.
duan-buffett-lunch.coda: The manufacturer was Duan Yongping. The young man was Colin Huang, who later founded Pinduoduo.

blackberry-iphone-2007.title: BlackBerry Saw the Flaws
